data.summary: Vascular & ulcers · 10 viva questions with answers
data.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Lipodermatosclerosis** (Vascular & ulcers)_

**Q1. Define lipodermatosclerosis (LDS).**
- Chronic sclerosing lobular/septal panniculitis of the lower legs due to chronic venous insufficiency (sclerosing panniculitis, hypodermitis sclerodermiformis); a C4b sign in CEAP classification
- Middle-aged and older women, obesity, venous hypertension

**Q2. Describe acute and chronic phases.**
- Acute: painful, warm, erythematous, indurated plaque on medial lower leg above the malleolus — often mistaken for cellulitis (bilateral, not febrile, no response to antibiotics)
- Chronic: woody, bound-down induration with hyperpigmentation (haemosiderin), sharply demarcated from normal skin above; circumferential fibrosis with oedema above produces an 'inverted champagne-bottle' or 'inverted bowling-pin' leg
- Associated: varicose veins, stasis eczema, atrophie blanche, venous ulcers (risk ↑)

**Q3. Pathogenesis.**
- Venous hypertension → capillary leakage of fibrinogen → pericapillary fibrin cuffs, tissue hypoxia → fat necrosis and fibrosis; fibrinolytic dysfunction; TGF-β1-driven fibrosis

**Q4. Histopathology.**
- Early: septal lymphocytic infiltrate, ischaemic fat necrosis in centre of lobules
- Late: septal fibrosis/sclerosis, lipomembranous (membranocystic) fat necrosis (feathery eosinophilic membranes lining cystic spaces), haemosiderin, stasis changes (lobular proliferation of thick-walled capillaries)
- Biopsy discouraged — poor healing and ulcer risk; diagnosis is clinical

**Q5. Differential diagnosis.**
- Acute: cellulitis (unilateral, fever, raised markers), erythema nodosum, morphoea, DVT, panniculitis (lupus profundus, pancreatic)
- Chronic: morphoea profunda, necrobiosis lipoidica, pretibial myxoedema (Graves'), scleroderma, eosinophilic fasciitis, elephantiasis nostras

**Q6. Investigations.**
- Venous duplex ultrasound for reflux/obstruction, ABPI before compression, Doppler to exclude DVT; blood counts/CRP to exclude infection

**Q7. Management.**
- Compression therapy (graduated stockings 30–40 mmHg; bandages initially) — mainstay; leg elevation, exercise, weight loss
- Treat venous reflux: endovenous ablation, sclerotherapy, surgery
- Drugs: pentoxifylline, stanozolol/danazol (anabolic steroids — fibrinolytic; side effects limit use), oxandrolone, aspirin; intralesional triamcinolone for acute painful areas; NSAIDs/analgesia
- Avoid trauma and biopsy; treat stasis eczema

**Q8. Prognosis.**
- Chronic progressive condition; acute pain improves with compression; increased risk of venous ulceration

**Q9. What is the CEAP clinical class of LDS and its significance?**
- C4b (with atrophie blanche) — advanced chronic venous disease with high risk of ulceration (C5–C6); indicates need for duplex assessment and treatment of reflux

**Q10. What is atrophie blanche and livedoid vasculopathy?**
- Atrophie blanche: ivory-white stellate atrophic scars with telangiectasia and pigmentation around ankles — end result of venous disease or livedoid vasculopathy
- Livedoid vasculopathy: thrombo-occlusive (not inflammatory) disease of dermal vessels with painful purpuric ulcers on ankles (summer), healing as atrophie blanche; associations — thrombophilia (factor V Leiden, protein C/S deficiency, raised lipoprotein(a), hyperhomocysteinaemia); treat with antiplatelets/ rivaroxaban, pentoxifylline, IVIG

## Quick spotter facts
- Inverted champagne-bottle leg with woody induration — lipodermatosclerosis
- Bilateral 'cellulitis' not responding to antibiotics — think acute LDS
- Avoid biopsy

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Venous disease; panniculitis). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._
